questions.prompt: What is the key difference between a process and a thread?

options.text: Threads in the same process share memory; processes have separate memory
Processes are always faster than threads
Threads can only run on one CPU core

questions.explanation: Processes are isolated by the operating system. Threads inside one process share its memory, which makes communication cheap but invites race conditions.

questions.prompt: Two threads each add 1 to a shared counter 1,000 times without a lock. The final value is 1,874. What happened?

options.text: A race condition: some read-add-write steps interleaved and overwrote each other
A deadlock: the threads stopped early

questions.explanation: Incrementing is read, add, write. When two threads read the same old value, one update is lost. A lock or an atomic increment fixes it.
questions.hint: Look at the table in the lesson where two threads both read 5.

questions.prompt: An event-loop server suddenly gets slow for every user after a new feature that resizes uploaded images inside the request handler. Why?

options.text: Image resizing is CPU work that blocks the single loop thread, so all other requests wait
The images use too much network bandwidth

questions.explanation: Event loops stay fast only when handlers return quickly. Heavy CPU work must move to worker threads or a separate service.

options.text: Always acquire multiple locks in the same global order
Hold locks for as short a time as possible
Use timeouts when waiting for a lock

questions.explanation: A consistent order removes the circular wait, short critical sections reduce the chance of conflict, and timeouts let a thread back off and retry. More threads don't help and can make contention worse.

questions.prompt: A service uses a pool of 100 threads. Each request blocks for 50 ms waiting on the database and uses almost no CPU. Roughly what's the maximum throughput?

options.text: Unlimited, since the CPU is idle

questions.explanation: Each thread finishes 1 / 0.05 s = 20 requests per second, and 100 threads give 2,000 per second. This is Little's Law: concurrency = throughput × latency.
